src/services/api/accountService.ts.note: PARTIAL. Its three WRITERS are ported: createAccount:223-287, updateAccount:289-336 and deleteAccount:338-372 (a soft close, which the seam already renamed closeAccount) are crates/wealth-core/src/verbs/{create,update,close}_account.rs. They port no Postgres function because there is none — accounts is written directly over PostgREST — so PHASE3-PLAN D-2 makes THIS FILE the oracle, transcribed key for key and default for default into lib/verb-postgres.mjs and run against the same payload by 25 verb-specs/account-*.spec.mjs, plus crates/wealth-core/tests/account_family.rs for the half with no cloud counterpart (B-1 across all three verbs, C-3 through the create, the audit trail the cloud does not write, and the guard table). Five divergences are declared, each with a spec, and every one is the local edition keeping an invariant the cloud's direct writes do not: the create takes one money figure rather than two, the update refuses a stated balance by name, an opening-balance edit moves the balance with it, a write that matches no row is a refusal rather than a silent success, and every write is audited. The reads (getAccounts, getClosedAccounts) are ported as crate::verbs::reads. Still outstanding here: getAccountById and subscribeToAccounts.

src/services/api/investmentService.ts.evidence: THE LAST UNPORTED REGION OF THE DATA LAYER, and slice 31 is where it joined the seam. The four writes and the read below this line are unchanged — the same SELECTED_COLUMNS, the same .eq() pairs, the same refusals — and what changed is who calls them: DataServiceImpl does, on its cloud branch, exactly as it delegates budgets and goals to PlanningService. pages/Investments.tsx asks dataPort and resolves no identity at all. The pure half (the types, INVESTMENT_ASSET_TYPES and toHolding) was lifted into src/services/investments/holding.ts so that a device bundle can read it — the slice 27 arrangement backupService.ts has with backup/format.ts — and every name is re-exported here, so not one of the importers moved. The local half is crates/wealth-core/src/verbs/{create,update,delete}_investment.rs plus apply_investment_prices.rs and reads.rs::list_investments, over crates/wealth-core/src/row/investment.rs and the new crates/wealth-core/src/scaled.rs — a SECOND fixed-point boundary at 1e8, because a unit price is a rate rather than an amount and numeric(10,2) was rounding £32.775 to £32.78 nightly until migration 20260809120000. cost_basis is DERIVED on both engines (quantity × averageCost, rounded half-away-from-zero to match numeric(10,2)) and neither takes one from a caller. Proved by 18 Rust tests in tests/investment_family.rs, eleven differential specs in scripts/local-sqlite/verb-specs/investment-*.spec.mjs and money2-*.spec.mjs (two of them DECLARED divergences: divergence 10's audit trail, and M-2 — a ninth decimal place rounded by numeric(20,8) and refused by Scaled8, plus the int64 cliff schema.sql called 'deliberate and tested' and which had no test until now), and seven contract rules that run on all three engines with B-12 declaring the one that has nowhere to keep a holding.

src/services/api/planningService.ts.reason: cloud-only — WRITE-PATHS slice 5e retired this file's local half: every operation now requires a configured Supabase client and a resolved owner, and refuses by name otherwise (the branches that wrote encrypted localStorage are deleted, not disabled). What is left is the Supabase transport for budgets/goals/categories — PostgREST queries, column mapping, and the migrate_categories_atomic / delete_unused_categories / merge_categories calls — which a local edition has no twin for. What changed in slice 22 is that this file became an ORACLE without becoming a porting item: PHASE3-PLAN D-2 makes the WRITER the thing a verb ports when there is no RPC to port, so createBudget/updateBudget/deleteBudget/createGoal/updateGoal/deleteGoal are transcribed key for key into lib/verb-postgres.mjs and run against the same payload as crates/wealth-core/src/verbs/{create,update,delete}_{budget,goal}.rs by 28 verb-specs/{budget,goal}-*.spec.mjs, with crates/wealth-core/tests/planning_writes.rs holding the half that has no cloud counterpart. Three of its lines were surprising enough to be pinned from both sides: createBudget fills in start_date and name after the mapper because both columns are NOT NULL; budgetToDb writes name whenever EITHER name or categoryId is present, so moving a budget to another category renames it; and createGoal's `currentAmount ?? 0` is where contract rule 49's opening figure comes from. The status stays out-of-scope because the TRANSPORT is still cloud-only. The budget/goal/category RULES it used to mirror are in scope elsewhere and stay there: the browser-storage engine is src/services/api/dataService.ts (pending), the operation contracts are src/services/port/dataPort.ts (pending), and the RPCs' behaviour is owned by their migrations (each dispositioned in its own entry).

src/services/api/simpleAccountService.ts.note: RETIRED FROM PRODUCTION — zero production importers after WRITE-PATHS slice A: the boot read and the account subscription moved to the seam in slice R, and the signed-in create followed once accountService's insert learned to send the sort code, account number, opening balance date and notes (createAccount is deleted here). Three test files still import it: services/__tests__/accountMapping.test.tsx (reads a row through both services to prove the one mapper cannot drift), services/__tests__/dataService.test.ts (pins one retired behaviour against the seam that replaced it) and its own suite. Deleting the file means deciding what replaces that second opinion, which is its own piece of work; until then D-5 stays pending against accountService, which is where the behaviour now lives.

src/services/api/suggestionDismissalServ.evidence: Both WRITERS are ported: dismiss:88-118 and restore:121-137 are crates/wealth-core/src/verbs/{dismiss,restore}_suggestion.rs, and list:61-81 was ported as crate::verbs::reads in slice 15. They port no Postgres function because there is none — suggestion_dismissals is written directly over PostgREST — so PHASE3-PLAN D-2 makes THIS FILE the oracle, transcribed key for key INCLUDING ITS CONTROL FLOW into lib/verb-postgres.mjs (the insert, the 23505 catch, and the find that answers with the row already there rather than updating it) and run against the same payload by 10 verb-specs/{dismiss,restore}-*.spec.mjs, plus crates/wealth-core/tests/dismissal_writes.rs for the half with no cloud counterpart. The private find:139-156 has no separate port: it IS the pre-check, which one IMMEDIATE SQLite transaction makes indistinguishable from the cloud's caught violation. Three decisions are pinned from both sides: idempotence is FIRST WINS and not an upsert, so dismissed_at goes on meaning "when you first said no" and the subjects stay the first caller's (20260806180000:127-128); restore is a DELETE and never a flag, keyed by (kind, subject_key) and never by id, because the screen offering undo has never seen a dismissal row; and NEITHER VERB AUDITS — the one family in the crate that agrees with the cloud about the trail, argued on the merits at 20260806180000:73-79 rather than inherited, because divergence 10 turns on money living in four columns and a dismissal has no figure in either engine. One divergence is declared with a spec: subject ids are a FOREIGN KEY in a file where the cloud's uuid[] has only a column comment, so a refusal naming no transaction is refused here and stored there. This slice also closed the schema gap this file's own DismissalKind exposed — scripts/local-sqlite/schema.sql admitted four of the seven kinds, which would have made Settings → Payee cleanup unable to save on a local ledger and would have refused a cloud backup carrying one payee dismissal WHOLE.

src/services/api/transactionService.ts.note: Holds D-4's latent third split writer (:916-981), which PHASE1 §7 puts out of scope — the RPC is the specification, not this mirror. The rest of the file is in scope.

src/services/backup/format.ts.note: A FILE MOVE, not a port. Slice 27 lifted the pure format half out of backupService.ts — the tag a file carries, the entities and their order, buildBackupBundle, validateBackupBundle, remapBackupIds, RESTORE_STEPS and rowsForStep — so that a desktop bundle can read and write the backup format without a Supabase client in its module scope (the obligation localDataPort.ts's BackupFormat recorded, and PHASE3-PLAN §5's two bundle greps, which src/services/local/__tests__/deviceDocument.cloudFree.test.ts now runs over the import graph). The DISPOSITION is deliberately unchanged: the same ids that were pending against backupService.ts are pending here, because moving a rule between files discharges nothing. What did change is that the local edition now uses these exact functions rather than a copy of them — LocalDataPort is constructed with them and localCore.contract.test.ts's backup round trip exercises them against a real .db file — which is why crates/wealth-core/src/lib.rs says remapBackupIds is deliberately NOT ported to Rust: a second implementation of one format is a file that exports what it cannot import.

src/services/conflictResolutionService.t.reason: phase 2 — PHASE1 §7: dormant (nothing dispatches CONFLICT_DETECTED_EVENT) and Phase 1 has no sync, so there are no conflicts to resolve. TS-C1/TS-C2 become the merge policy in the cloud↔local sync design. Preserve the file; do not port it.

src/services/import/msMoney/cloudPlan.ts.note: A FILE MOVE, not a port, on backup/format.ts's precedent and for the same reason: planCloudImport is pure and is the ONE planner all three engines share, and it lived in a module whose scope reaches storageAdapter and the app's cloud-bound logger. The two rules the write path shares with the planner came with it (reconciledFromMoney and the column name executeCloudPlan's fallback strips), because the planner uses them and a planner that imported the writer would restore the import the move exists to break. msMoneyImport.ts re-exports all of it; the pending ids are unchanged because a move is not a port.

src/services/import/msMoney/feedOverlap..evidence: crates/wealth-core/src/admission/feed_overlap.rs — both passes, the handover and its two refusals. 25 admission-specs/overlap-*.spec.mjs against this module, plus crates/wealth-core/tests/admission.rs for the property the differential cannot carry (a feed row with an unreadable date matches nothing; its position in the SORT is undefined in this module, whose comparator returns NaN, so no spec asserts it). src/services/import/msMoney/transform.ts.note: PARTIAL. Its reconciliation policy (TS-I9, transform.ts:350 and :357) is ported as ClearedPolicy::MoneyStatusScale and proved by admission-specs/cleared-*money* against THIS module, driven through transformMsMoneyExport. Money's cs is a three-value SCALE and answers BOTH of the app's flags since migration 20260810200000: cleared is 1-or-2 (marked), reconciled is 2 alone (committed), so the port carries decide() and decide_reconciled() and the four specs assert the pair. The rest of the transform is the 1,300-line importer PHASE1-PLAN §3.1 explicitly keeps in TypeScript.

src/services/investmentEnhancementServic.reason: deleted: invented its own ESG scores (Math.random), beta, Sharpe and benchmarks

src/services/local/coreTransport.ts.evidence: The one door between TypeScript and the ledger crate, and it holds no money rule because it moves no money: a verb string and a payload out, one {ok,error} envelope back. What it does own is the fault/refusal distinction the seam depends on — a refusal keeps the crate's own prose verbatim (seam rule 4, rendered straight into the UI), a fault gets a sentence of its own, and code/hint ride non-enumerably so that nothing can branch on them. Proved by src/services/port/__tests__/localCore.contract.test.ts, which drives every read the suite makes through the spawn transport against a real .db file, and by the three rules that use createUnreadable: loadBoot, loadBootTransactions and getAccountBalances must RESOLVE when the file will not open, which only happens if a storage fault really does arrive here as a rejection.

src/services/local/deviceIdentity.ts.evidence: Who you are on a device: the uuid in the open file's one `users` row, published once when the document is opened and read by everything above the seam. It moves no money and stores none — what it owns is the ANSWER to a question the cloud answers with Clerk and a database lookup (userIdService, whose module scope reaches a Supabase client on its first line and which a desktop can neither import nor use, because there is nothing to translate). PHASE3-PLAN D-5 settles the identity of a LEDGER and slices 18 and 27 built both ends: LocalDataPort is constructed with an owner and puts it on every verb, and document.rs mints a v4 uuid at create and reads it back at open, refusing by name a file with no login row and a file with two. This is the middle, and it is deliberately a value with a lifetime rather than a service with a cache: a device has ONE id, it cannot change while the file is open, and an identity that could be refreshed would be one that could be refreshed to something else. Module scope for the same reason `preferences` is a singleton — the callers are useState initialisers scattered across pages that mount at different times — set in exactly one place (openDeviceDocument, AFTER the port has refused a non-uuid owner, so the app above is never told an identity the engine below rejected) and cleared in one (forgetDeviceIdentity, which is what close_ledger means up here, and which src/test/setup.ts calls between cases). Proved by src/services/local/__tests__/deviceDocument.test.ts: the published owner is the FILE's, nothing is published before a ledger is opened and requireDeviceOwner says so rather than guessing, a second open replaces it, a close forgets it, and a malformed owner publishes nothing at all. It is load-bearing rather than decorative because the boot ASKS it — bootDeviceLedger attaches the preferences service to requireDeviceOwner()'s answer and refuses when it disagrees with the document being booted, which is the case a second open would otherwise turn into a silent cross-file write.

src/services/local/preferencesTransport..evidence: The third implementation of PreferencesTransport, and the reason a device's settings are in the backup at all: the cloud keeps them in a user_preferences row, the browser keeps them in the service's own mirror, and this keeps them in the ledger file, over two verbs (read_preferences, write_preferences). It handles no money. What it owns is the translation and one rule that lives nowhere else: it REFUSES a user id that is not the open file's owner. A file can legitimately hold a second login's rows — a restored backup from an account that had two — and there is no RLS to narrow an answer afterwards, so passing the id through would answer `null` for a login the file does not hold, which PreferencesService.attach reads as 'no settings yet' and answers with THE LIFT: this window's whole document written into the file under somebody else's id, refused by the foreign key at a moment nobody is watching, after which the person's settings silently stop being saved. It also keeps null and {} apart, because attach branches on exactly that difference, and treats a MISSING key as a fault rather than as an absence for the same reason. Its types come from services/preferences/document.ts rather than from preferencesService.ts even though the import would be erased — this module is reachable from the desktop's root and deviceDocument.cloudFree.test.ts walks that graph on every run. Proved three ways: src/services/local/__tests__/preferencesTransport.test.ts (10 tests) for the translation and both directions of the refusal, src/services/port/__tests__/localCore.preferences.test.ts against REAL files through the REAL crate (a document that survives the file being closed and reopened, two logins in one file kept apart, and a dashboardKeyAccounts preference whose account ids are followed through a restore to the accounts they became), and scripts/local-sqlite/verb-specs/preferences-* which runs the same payloads against the cloud's own supabasePreferencesTransport transcribed into SQL.

src/services/local/deviceDataPort.ts.evidence: The DEVICE edition's one production entry point to the seam, and the twin of src/services/port/index.ts. It handles no money and holds no rule about any: it is one statement — `export const dataPort: DataPort = requireDeviceDocument().port` — plus the re-export of the seam's type vocabulary, and it exists so that shared UI can import `@data` and get whichever engine this build is. That indirection is the whole edition gating (docs/edition-gating.md): the web build resolves `@data` to services/port/index.ts and a desktop build resolves it to this file, so neither bundle contains the other's engine because neither bundle's graph can reach it — which a branch inside one file could never have achieved, and which PHASE3-PLAN §5's two bundle greps would have failed on the first build. The one RULE it does own is an ORDER, and it is stated by throwing: the port is resolved at module scope, so a desktop that imported the application before a ledger was open would bind every screen to nothing, and requireDeviceDocument refuses with a sentence naming src/desktop/main.tsx rather than answering something empty. Proved by src/services/local/__tests__/deviceDataPort.test.ts (the same object as the open document's port, not a copy; the device capabilities; the refusal before a ledger is open and the sentence that names where the order is kept; a second open following the window), by src/services/__tests__/dataAlias.test.ts (this module and its cloud twin declare the same type vocabulary and the same single value export, and all six configs that resolve a module agree about which file `@data` is), and by src/desktop/__tests__/desktopEntry.cloudFree.test.ts, which walks the desktop entry's import graph with `@data` resolved the way apps/desktop/vite.config.ts resolves it and fails if services/api/dataService is reachable. The web bundle is unchanged by its existence: 158 built artefacts byte-identical across the slice.

src/services/local/deviceDocument.ts.evidence: The desktop's object graph, assembled in one place: the invoke transport, LocalDataPort, the REAL backup format and the REAL .mny planner out of the two modules slice 27 lifted, and the device boot. It holds one rule of its own and it is an ORDER — prepareCategories() is awaited before loadBoot(), which is where this engine keeps the seam's 'categories resolve before any transaction or budget read'. The cloud keeps that inside its own loadBoot; a file cannot, because load_boot is ONE crossing of ONE transaction and seeding is a deliberate act rather than a side effect of looking at a file (localDataPort.ts says so at prepareCategories, and the contract suite spies on the method and fails the composite if the boot reached it). Proved by src/services/local/__tests__/deviceDocument.test.ts, which asserts the two verbs arrive in that order and that the second waits for the first — a slow seed, so an implementation that started both at once fails — plus the owner reaching every payload, the uuid refusal before anything is asked, and the format being the same function objects the cloud export calls rather than copies of them. It is also the root PHASE3-PLAN §5's two bundle greps are run from: deviceDocument.cloudFree.test.ts walks the runtime import graph from this module and fails if a Supabase client, the browser storage adapter, the app's logger or any node: built-in is reachable, naming the chain — and proves the walker can fail by finding all three from backupService.ts. Measured against the built bundle too: apps/desktop/dist is 79.7 kB raw / 27.4 kB gzipped and contains zero occurrences of supabase, indexedDB, storageAdapter, clerk or sentry. Slice 28 gave it two more things to assemble and one more ordering rule. openDeviceDocument now answers with the THREE shapes one open file has above the seam — the engine (LocalDataPort), the identity (the file's owner, published to deviceIdentity.ts) and the settings store (localPreferencesTransport over the SAME CoreTransport the port uses, because there is one connection behind one mutex and two transports would only be two objects a later caller could point at two documents). The ordering rule is that useTransport precedes attach: attach resolves the store when it runs, so the other order would read a person's settings out of whichever store the previous session left configured — on a desktop that is the cloud's, which is absent, so the whole document would come back as 'nothing saved yet' and the LIFT would overwrite the file's real settings with this window's defaults. It also diverges from the cloud deliberately in awaiting the attach where AppContextSupabase fires `void attach(...)`: the cloud's reason is a network round trip, a device has none, and awaiting buys a first paint that is the person's own theme and currency rather than the defaults corrected a frame later. It is STARTED before the seed and awaited after the boot, so its crossing overlaps rather than delays, and it cannot fail the boot. All of it is proved by src/services/local/__tests__/deviceDocument.test.ts (20 tests): the store and the id the service is bound to, the call order, the overlap, a boot that still succeeds when the attach does not, a boot given no service leaving the settings alone, and the refusal to boot a document that is not the ledger this window has open.

src/services/local/mappers/columns.ts.evidence: The columns of a transaction, of a split line, of an account, of a category and — since slice 22 — of a budget and a goal, declared ONCE and read in both directions — the discipline localCore.fixtureFile.ts already imposes on its own writer and reader, for the reason it gives: two independent conversions that are wrong in the same way agree perfectly, so a real disagreement between them looks like a fixture bug. It is also where a money number leaves as text: String(amount), never toFixed (which ROUNDS, and would turn M-1's refusal of a sub-penny amount into a silent invention of half a penny) and never *100 (float arithmetic on money, which is banned outright under src/services/local and greppably absent). Proved by src/services/port/__tests__/localCore.contract.test.ts against a real .db file: the money rules use figures IEEE-754 gets wrong (0.1 + 0.2, -70.1 - -70.3, 10.1 + 20.2 + 0.3) and read the balances back through an independent mapper, and M-1 asserts that -0.125 is refused with nothing written. It is also where the table's own LIMIT is written down: one column, one field, so a goal's progress/currentAmount pair and its status/isActive/achieved trio are NOT here — they are assembly, and writes.ts owns them beside the account create's openingBalance || balance || 0 for the same reason. The single table is also what caught the wire name of the type column: the crate's Rust field is `kind` and serde renames it back to `type`, and reading `kind` off an answer had silently typed every local account 'other' and every transaction 'expense' since slice 18.

src/services/investments/holding.ts.evidence: The pure half of investmentService, lifted at slice 31 so that three readers can have it and only one of them may see a Supabase client: dataPort.ts (types, erased), services/local/mappers and localDataPort (INVESTMENT_ASSET_TYPES and toHolding, at RUNTIME, in a desktop bundle), and investmentService itself, which re-exports every name so no importer moved. toHolding is ONE mapper for BOTH engines — the arrangement rows.ts already has for an account, and possible because the crate's list_investments answers with the cloud's own SELECTED_COLUMNS. It accepts a figure as a JSON number (PostgREST) or as a decimal string (the crate) and goes through Decimal in both cases, so no float exists on this path whichever engine answered. marketValue is COMPUTED here rather than read: the column exists in both schemas and neither writes it, because a stored copy of quantity × price goes stale the moment the price does.

src/services/backup/browserCoverage.ts.evidence: WHAT THE BROWSER'S STORE CANNOT KEEP, declared once and read twice — by localBackupService, which builds the stored:false half of LOCAL_BACKUP_BINDINGS from it, and by dataService, which answers capabilities().cannotKeep with it SYNCHRONOUSLY in a render. It exists because a second declaration would have been free to drift from the first, and drift in exactly this list is the bug it was extracted for: RestoreBackupModal warned, before a restore, that a file held rows the target could not keep — built from the browser's bindings, chosen by backupTarget !== 'login', which a DEVICE also matches. A ledger file keeps all fourteen tables and would have been told its own budgets could not be restored. The module imports two TYPES and nothing else, so it is erased to one frozen array: the arrow points from the heavy module to the light one and never the other way. Completeness is still localBackupService's, whose Record<BackupEntity, …> makes a missing table a compile error.

src/services/local/localDataPort.ts.evidence: The local edition's half of the seam, WHOLE: eleven reads, the loadBoot composite, the capability descriptor, the lifecycle, and every write group — the sixteen of slice 19, the three ACCOUNT writes of slice 20, the four CATEGORY writes of slice 21 with prepareCategories beside them, the six PLANNING writes of slice 22, the two DISMISSAL writes of slice 23, the five RECONCILIATION and ARCHIVE writes of slice 24, slice 25's re-point and BACKUP ROUND TRIP, and slice 26's importMsMoney. Each one is a verb over the transport, with the owner added in exactly one place (#ask), which is what makes seam rule 1 a property of the code rather than a habit. It computes no money at all: a figure is parsed once in mappers/values.ts on the way in and rendered once in mappers/columns.ts on the way out, and PHASE3-PLAN R-7 stays greppable — no /100 and no *100 anywhere under src/services/local. Proved by src/services/port/__tests__/localCore.contract.test.ts, where every rule of the suite runs green on this engine against a real .db file driven through the real Rust crate, with NONE skipped: the balances that agree with the client sum to the penny, the import that lands as a prefix and reports rather than throws, the twenty split and transfer refusals down to which fires first, D-7's refusal of a key outside the update allow-list, M-1's refusal of a sub-penny amount with nothing written, the wipe that leaves the file agreeing it is empty, and collect, wipe, restore, collect — the journey a person actually makes and the only one that can prove a backup is a backup. THE SURFACE IS NOW PROVED TWICE. The class says `implements DataPort` and tsc -b compiles this module, so the compiler checks all fifty-six operations; and the contract suite's surface rule walks DATA_PORT_OPERATIONS against the object a harness really assembled, which no annotation can. contract.ts's NOT_YET ratchet — the per-engine list of operations not yet written, checked in both directions, counted and monotone-shrinking (41, 25, 22, 17, 11, 9, 4, 1) — reached zero at slice 26 and was DELETED rather than left holding an empty array, along with its ceiling and the skip-by-name branch in the rule helper. The account, category, planning and dismissal families are the ones whose verbs port no Postgres function at all (PHASE3-PLAN D-2: the cloud writes those tables directly over PostgREST), so their oracle is the TypeScript writer, transcribed into SQL in lib/verb-postgres.mjs and run against the same payload. repointTransfer is the opposite kind: a port of the newest RPC in the schema (20260810140000), whose crossover rule — each leg filed under the OTHER account's To/From category — is derived from the new pairing on both rows rather than patched on one, and whose six differential specs compare it against that RPC payload for payload. The backup pair is a third kind again: collectBackup ports a TypeScript READER (backupService.collectBackupBundle's walk of fourteen tables) and deliberately ports only the read half — buildBackupBundle, remapBackupIds, RESTORE_STEPS and rowsForStep are INJECTED into the port rather than imported by it, because they are the one format all three engines share and backupService carries a Supabase client a desktop bundle may not. B-10 is where the two engines are allowed to differ and the seam says so: the cloud restores in chunks that each commit alone, this is one call in one transaction, and the three RestoreOutcome fields that shape could not honestly guess at were answered rather than invented — per-step counts from the verb's positional answer, an EMPTY notStoredLocally because a file holds all fourteen tables, and a stated sentence when a file carries preferences this edition cannot store yet. importMsMoney is a FOURTH kind and writes no new path at all: it is wipeAllFinancialData() then restoreBackup(), composed over planCloudImport — the same planner the cloud migration runs, INJECTED for the same reason the format is, because its module reaches storageAdapter and the app's cloud-bound logger. The crate hands money over as a fixed two-place decimal string (money.rs refuses a JSON number outright, because a JSON number is an IEEE-754 double by the time any parser has read it) and this is where it becomes the app's number — once, with no arithmetic on either side of it. Also the date boundary: an ISO timestamp becomes a Date, and a 'YYYY-MM-DD' day becomes a Date at NOON so that no zone west of Greenwich renames the day a statement is dated. Proved through mappers/rows.ts by src/services/port/__tests__/localCore.contract.test.ts, whose fixtures are chosen so that IEEE-754 gets the sums wrong (0.1 + 0.2, -70.1, 30.6): the balance rule compares the crate's derived figure against the client's own, to the penny.

src/services/local/mappers/writes.ts.evidence: The app's drafts, patches and split lines on their way INTO a ledger file, each through the one column table in columns.ts so nothing can be written under a name it is not read back under. It holds two decisions worth naming. A CREATE is filtered to the verb's own arguments (which reproduces what create_transaction_atomic does with the same jsonb blob — reads the keys it knows, ignores the rest — and is what keeps an ordinary Omit<Transaction,'id'> from being refused for carrying isSplit), while an UPDATE is passed through whole, because divergence D-7 gives this engine 'refuses' for a key outside the allow-list and it can only refuse what it is shown. Proved by src/services/port/__tests__/localCore.contract.test.ts: the D-7 rule sends `archived` on an update and asserts a rejection with the row unchanged, the import rules assert every written row arrives needsReview true and the account moves by 30.60 to the penny, and the split rules assert the five-key line payload down to which refusal fires first. The rule is not 'creates filter and updates do not': it is do what the cloud's own mapper does with an unknown key, which is a different answer for each of the three entities that has one. This file is also where the default category tree crosses the seam (defaultCategorySeed), so src/data/defaultCategories.ts stays the ONE list all three engines start a fresh store from and the crate holds no copy of it. The second decision is the account create's ONE money figure: Omit<Account,'id'> carries a balance AND an opening balance, an account with no transactions cannot honour two different figures without breaking B-1, and this file folds them the way accountService.createAccount folds them (openingBalance || balance || 0) so the verb has no second money argument to send the loser to. contract.ts's ACCOUNT_BALANCE_AT_BIRTH declares what each engine then does. supabase/migrations/20260810200000_marki.note: UNAPPLIED at the time of writing — the owner applies migrations himself — so it cannot be "ported" against a live definition the way its neighbours are. Splits Money's two states apart: transactions.is_reconciled (nullable, no backfill, so history keeps NULL and its is_cleared answers) and accounts.last_reconciled_balance. Four rules for a local port: set_transactions_cleared keeps a commitment when marking and clears it when unmarking; finalize_reconciliation commits ONLY rows whose is_reconciled is explicitly false and records the day and the ending balance in the same transaction (zero is a balance, absent is not); archive_transactions_before judges COALESCE(is_reconciled, is_cleared); and the archive sweep trigger fires on is_reconciled, never on the mark. scripts/local-sqlite/schema.sql does not carry either column yet.

supabase/migrations/20260810090000_impor.note: UNAPPLIED at the time of writing — the owner applies migrations himself — so it cannot be "ported" against a live definition the way its neighbours are. Four functions are restated here (import_transactions_atomic, import_bank_transactions_atomic, update_transaction_atomic, confirm_transaction_categories) and the local core's verbs for all four will need the needs_review column that scripts/local-sqlite/schema.sql already carries. Three rules to port with them: both importers write it TRUE unconditionally; the updater honours it only when the caller states it and never derives it; confirming a suggested category clears it.
